answers.answer: These are two INDEPENDENT dials, and my spec treats them as separate hard gates that BOTH must pass — but it does not spell out the four-quadrant precedence the question asks for, so this is a partial. What the spec says: 25% USTER (on CVm% + IPI) is the mainstream EVENNESS bar for mass acrylic/cotton (never 5% on a mass lot), and ICI >=3-4 post-wash is a SEPARATE pilling gate; the accept/reject verdict 'refuses a lot failing any hard gate' (capability 6). So the resolution of the two cases you pose is actually clean by the 'any hard gate' rule: a lot passing ICI but sitting at ~30% USTER FAILS (misses the 25% evenness bar); a lot passing 25% USTER but failing ICI FAILS (misses the pilling gate). Neither 'dominates' — both are pass/fail gates and either failure rejects the lot. On the deeper question — is 25% USTER ever TOO LOOSE to hold the pilling floor? — evenness (CVm%/IPI) and pilling are largely decoupled: pilling is driven by the five spinning dials (staple, twist, ply, fineness/dpf, blend) plus the anti-pill/higher-dpf grade, NOT primarily by USTER percentile. My glossary 'five spinning dials' and the A2 competency question ('lives on the anti-pill grade and the ICI post-wash gate') make the ICI gate, not USTER, the pilling guarantor. So there is no true contradiction: a lot can be evenness-mediocre yet low-pill, or evenness-clean yet high-pill, which is exactly why BOTH gates exist. GAP: the spec never writes out the explicit 'either-fails-rejects, they are decoupled, USTER is not the pilling lever' logic; it is inferable from capability 6 + the five-dials glossary but not stated as a precedence rule.
answers.grounded_in: capability 'deliver a labeled-estimate yarn cost read and accept/reject verdict' (method: 'composing the USTER clause + pilling gate + composition verify + AQL sample into a single accept/reject call that refuses a lot failing any hard gate'); glossary 'USTER percentile (25% bar)', 'five spinning dials', 'ICI pilling gate'; conflicts_and_dominance 'tighter spec versus quotability'; competency_questions_covered ('A2 ... lives on the anti-pill grade and the ICI post-wash gate').

answers.answer: Honest answer: my spec names TWO 'dominant constraints' and does NOT give an explicit tie-break when they collide — this is a genuine decision-procedure gap. The two are: (commercial) 'the dye-lot MOQ sizes the brand' and (quality) 'the post-wash pilling gate dominates any anti-pill adjective.' Decision_procedure step 7 says to 'name the dominant constraint resolved' (singular), and capability 6 says 'refuses a lot failing any hard gate' — from which the collision you pose IS actually resolvable, but by a rule the spec implies rather than states. Worked collision: suppose the only bought-dyed stock shade that meets the dye-lot MOQ (so the line is commercially feasible in that colour) is a fibre/twist grade that FAILS ICI >=3-4 post-wash. Resolution under 'refuses a lot failing any hard gate': the QUALITY gate is a HARD accept/reject gate — a lot failing ICI is rejected outright, so you do NOT launch that colour; you find another stock shade that passes both, or drop the colour (accepting a MORE colour-starved line). So in a true collision the pilling gate is a veto (hard reject), while the dye-lot MOQ is a SIZING constraint (it caps how many colours, not whether a failing lot is acceptable). That gives an implicit precedence: the pilling hard-gate REJECTS; the dye-lot MOQ then SIZES within the surviving passing options. But my spec never writes that ordering — it presents them as two co-equal 'dominant constraints,' which is the over-claim the question catches. They operate on different axes (one is a pass/fail quality veto, the other a commercial sizing cap), so they rarely truly conflict, but when they do the spec lacks an explicit 'quality veto first, then MOQ sizes' tie-break.
